commonMistakes: Do not write “seal the plate completely”. School plates are taped at a few points rather than sealed all the way around; this reduces contamination while avoiding strongly anaerobic conditions.
“Sterile” and “aseptic” are not interchangeable: sterile means free of living microorganisms; aseptic technique means procedures used to reduce contamination.

detailedExplanation: This topic is verified against The Tiffin Girls’ School Year 9 Biology Curriculum Outline 2026–27 and the corresponding AQA GCSE Biology 8461 content.
Bacteria can reproduce by binary fission. Under suitable conditions they can divide rapidly. Bacteria can be grown in nutrient broth or on agar plates.
When investigating bacteria, scientists try to grow an uncontaminated culture so that only the intended microorganism is present. Contamination can make results invalid and can create a safety risk.

Aseptic technique reduces contamination. Culture media and Petri dishes are sterilised before use. An inoculating loop is sterilised before transferring microorganisms. The lid is opened as little as possible. The plate is secured with tape but not completely sealed, stored upside down and, in school laboratories, incubated at no more than 25°C.
You must know how bacteria reproduce, how cultures are grown, why aseptic technique matters and the safety rules used in school laboratories.

Explain biological ideas as linked steps: name the structure or process, state what happens, and connect it to the effect on the cell, organism or ecosystem. Use precise scientific terms rather than everyday substitutes.

additionalSourceSections.heading: Why These Steps Matter
additionalSourceSections.body:
Aseptic flow: sterile agar/loop → sterilise and cool loop → lift lid slightly → inoculate/streak → re-sterilise between streak areas → replace lid → tape at a few points → invert → incubate at ≤25°C.
Purpose: reduce contamination while avoiding unsafe strongly anaerobic conditions.
